S7.excerpt: Abstract Global catastrophic risk (GCR) is the potential for an unprecedented worldwide catastrophe which eliminates more than a tenth of the population within decades. In the worst cases, this could lead to existential risk: the potential for global societal collapse or human extinction. There is an emerging consensus that the world now faces a non-trivial level of GCR. This century could see such a global calamity. Despite its importance to the future of humanity, GCR is understudied, although the field is rapidly advancing. This primer outlines the current state of knowledge on GCR, including the definitions, several of contributors to GCR (AI, climate change, nuclear weapons, pandemics, and natural hazards), how probabilities are estimated, and current challenges for the field.
S7.title: A Primer on Global Catastrophic Risk (GCR)

S14.excerpt: Abstract This paper estimates the medium- to long-term effects of the workfare program Construyendo Perú using a fuzzy regression discontinuity design and three comprehensive databases. The program helped raise employment and reduce inactivity for some groups, but these gains occurred mainly in lower-quality jobs (i.e., informal and paid below the poverty line). Participation did not improve job quality among lower-educated beneficiaries and pushed women, men, and higher-educated individuals into informal, low-earning jobs. These results suggest that the program’s shift from infrastructure- to service-sector-related projects during its last two years—which were less costly, of shorter duration, and offered no training—may explain the negative effects on participants’ job quality.
S14.title: Workfare Programs and Their Delivery System: Effectiveness of Construyendo Perú
